topic: Template Type Deduction for Array-to-Pointer Decay
explanation:
When an array is passed by value to a template function, it undergoes array-to-pointer decay before type deduction occurs. The deduced type for the template parameter will be a pointer type, not the original array type. This means all compile-time information about the array's size is lost during the process.

Scott Meyers emphasizes that this behavior stems from C's legacy rules and contributes to the common but mistaken belief that array and pointer types are interchangeable. He points out that template type deduction makes the distinction clear: passing an array by value fundamentally transforms its type into a pointer, erasing crucial size information that existed at the call site.

The mechanics are straightforward. Before the compiler attempts to deduce the template parameter `T` for a by-value parameter, it first applies the array-to-pointer decay rule to the argument. An argument of type `const char[13]` is converted to `const char*`. This resulting pointer type is then used for deduction, so `T` is deduced as `const char*`.

This has significant practical implications, especially when interacting with C-style APIs or arrays. If a generic function needs to know the size of an array passed to it, it cannot be passed by value. This is why many functions that operate on C-style arrays, like those in the C standard library, require a separate argument for the element count. Understanding this decay is crucial for writing correct generic code that handles raw arrays.

A common pitfall is assuming the template parameter will somehow capture the array type. A developer might try to use `sizeof` on the by-value parameter inside the template, expecting to get the size of the entire array. Instead, they will get the size of a pointer, which is a frequent source of bugs and subtle errors.
practical_example: When writing a generic logging function that accepts C-style strings, passing by value causes the string literal or char array to decay to a pointer. This allows the function to work generically with different character arrays, but it means the function cannot know the buffer's size at compile time and must rely on null termination.
keywords: array-to-pointer decay, template array decay, array size loss, template deduction array argument
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
